title: Building a 750+ CIBIL Score From Scratch
tagline: Your financial reputation as a number. What moves it, what wrecks it, and a concrete plan for a 22-year-old with no credit history to reach 750+ before they ever need a loan.
summary: What the CIBIL score is, the five factors that drive it, and a from-zero plan to reach 750+.

sections.title: What a CIBIL score is and why it matters

paragraphs: A **CIBIL score** is a 3-digit number from **300 to 900** that summarises how reliably you repay borrowed money. Lenders pull it before approving any loan or credit card. It's your financial reputation, quantified.

It matters long before you 'need' it. When Aarav eventually wants a car loan (his 2031 goal) or a home loan, the score decides two things: **whether** he's approved, and at **what interest rate**. A 780 score might get a car loan at 9%, while a 650 score gets 13% or a rejection — over a multi-lakh loan, that gap is tens of thousands of rupees.

items.label: Poor / risky — likely rejected or charged high rates
Fair — approved, but not the best rates
Good to excellent — best rates and limits

blocks.title: Myth: 'I've never borrowed, so my score must be great'
blocks.text: Wrong. No credit history means a score of NA/NH ('Not Applicable' / 'No History'), which lenders treat as unknown risk. You have to *build* a track record of responsible borrowing and repaying. A clean slate is not the same as a strong score.

sections.title: The five things that move your score

items.detail: Do you pay on time, in full, every time? A single missed payment can drop your score sharply and stays on the report for years. This one factor dominates.
How much of your available credit limit you use. Keep it under ~30%. On a ₹50,000 limit, try to keep the statement balance below ₹15,000 — high utilisation signals dependence on credit.
Older accounts help. This is why opening your first card early (and never closing it) is valuable — it ages into an asset.
A healthy blend of types (e.g. a card + later a small loan) is viewed slightly better than a single type. Minor factor — don't take loans just for this.
Each time you apply for credit, a 'hard enquiry' is logged. Many applications in a short span looks desperate and dings the score. Apply sparingly and deliberately.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Pay in full and on time (autopay the full amount), keep utilisation under 30%, keep your oldest card open forever, and don't apply for credit you don't need. Do these four things consistently and 750+ takes care of itself.

items.title: Get a 'starter' credit line
items.detail: With a thin file and a ₹20,000 income, a regular unsecured card may be declined. The reliable route is a SECURED credit card against a fixed deposit (you put, say, ₹15,000 in an FD and get a card with a limit near that). It reports to CIBIL exactly like a normal card, and the FD keeps earning interest.

items.title: Use it for small, regular spends
items.detail: Put one or two routine bills on it — a phone recharge, a subscription, some groceries. The goal is activity, not borrowing. Keep the statement balance well under 30% of the limit.

items.title: Set up autopay for the FULL amount
items.detail: Automate payment of the Total Amount Due, not the minimum. On-time, in-full payments are the single biggest score driver. Twelve perfect months build a strong foundation.

items.title: Be patient — scores build over months
items.detail: After ~6 months of clean usage a score appears; after ~12–18 months of perfect behaviour, 750+ is very achievable. There is no overnight hack — consistency is the entire strategy.

items.title: Check your report free, fix errors
items.detail: You're entitled to a free credit report each year (via CIBIL and other bureaus). Check it for errors — wrong defaults or accounts that aren't yours can unfairly drag your score, and you can dispute them.

blocks.title: What sabotages a young score
blocks.text: Missing even one due date, maxing out the card (high utilisation), applying for several cards/loans at once, or closing your only card. Also: being an 'add-on' user of someone else's card usually does NOT build your own history — you need credit in your own name.

cheatsheet: CIBIL score = 300–900; aim for 750+ for the best loan approvals and rates.
No credit history shows as NA/NH, not a high score — you must build a track record.
Biggest driver is payment history: pay in full and on time, every time.
Keep credit utilisation under ~30% of your limit.
From zero: a secured (FD-backed) card → small regular spends → autopay full amount → patience over 12–18 months.
Keep your oldest card open, avoid clustering credit applications, and check your free report for errors.

questions.prompt: Aarav, 22, has never borrowed anything and assumes his CIBIL score is excellent. Why is that assumption wrong, and what's the fix?
questions.hint: What does a lender see when there's no history at all?
answer: With no borrowing history, his score isn't high — it's **NA/NH (no history)**, which lenders read as unknown/unproven risk, not as proven reliability. A strong score is *earned* by demonstrating on-time, in-full repayment over time.

The fix is to build a track record: get a starter (likely secured/FD-backed) credit card, use it for small regular spends, and autopay the full bill every month. After 12–18 months of clean behaviour, he'll have an actual 750+ score backed by evidence.
keyPoints: Score must be earned via repayment record
Start with a secured card + perfect payments

questions.prompt: Aarav has a card with a ₹50,000 limit. In one month he spends ₹40,000 (he can pay it all in full) but worries about his score. What's the utilisation issue and how does he handle it?
questions.hint: Utilisation is measured against the limit, often at statement time.
answer: Even though he can pay in full, spending ₹40,000 on a ₹50,000 limit is **80% utilisation**, well above the ~30% guideline. The statement may report that high balance to CIBIL before he pays, temporarily denting his score by signalling heavy reliance on credit.

Two fixes: (1) make a part-payment *before* the statement date so the reported balance stays under ~₹15,000 (30%), or (2) spread spending or request a higher limit so the same spending is a smaller fraction of available credit. And of course, still pay the full amount by the due date.
keyPoints: Pre-pay before statement to lower reported balance
Or raise the limit / spread spend
Still pay full by due date

questions.prompt: Aarav reasons: 'I'll keep my CIBIL spotless by never getting a credit card at all.' Why might this backfire when he applies for a car loan in 2031?
questions.hint: What does the lender have to base their decision on?
answer: Avoiding all credit means he reaches 2031 with no credit history — NA/NH — so the car-loan lender has zero evidence of how he repays. That often leads to rejection or a higher interest rate, because unproven borrowers are treated as risky. Ironically, the 'safe' path of never borrowing leaves him *worse* positioned than someone who responsibly used a card for years.
The smarter play is to build the score deliberately and early with a low-risk secured card, so that by 2031 he has a long, clean history and qualifies for the best loan rate exactly when he needs it.
keyPoints: No card → no history → NA/NH in 2031
Leads to rejection or higher rate
Responsible early use beats total avoidance
Build the history before you need the loan
